remaining_concerns: Most of the file is treaty-status or policy-adoption evidence rather than proof of practical implementation or operational control.
The record is strong on formal non-nuclear positioning, but weaker on whether the cybersecurity and legal steps were executed effectively in 2022.
Retrospective NGO and technical-monitoring items add useful corroboration, but the core evidence still depends on official and treaty-record sources.
Several peace-process and official items show stated intent or institutional action, not proof of battlefield outcomes.
Humanitarian records document severe civilian harm and displacement, but usually do not assign direct presidential responsibility.
Attribution of external support and proxy dynamics remains contested in some reports, so those claims should stay cautious.
Much of the negative evidence concerns state responsibility by omission, tolerance, or emergency-rule abuse rather than direct presidential orders.
Eastern-conflict sources overlap heavily across displacement, civilian harm, and protection failures, so the retained set prioritizes synthesis over incident-by-incident repetition.
Press-freedom and protest-repression evidence is strong but still fragmented across multiple incidents and mixed attribution.
Evidence remains concentrated in a few mechanisms: emergency rule, election administration, and media space.
Most favorable items are procedural or corrective rather than proof of durable institutional change.
The Kabund arrest appears in multiple sources; only one is retained as the main incident, with the rest treated as duplicate or background material.
Several positive records are still policy intent or program design rather than observed delivery.
The rights picture is strong on repression, but much of it comes from NGO reporting and incident-based evidence.
Extractive-sector transparency improved, yet beneficial-ownership implementation remained incomplete at year-end.
Some social-protection and education gains are donor-mediated, so direct presidential causation is only partial.
Heavy dependence on humanitarian and sector-baseline evidence means ruler attribution remains indirect in several retained records.
UNICEF dominates the education and service-delivery evidence stream, though the set still stays within the 25 percent cap.
Several retained records are crisis-response or donor/IGO-supported interventions, so they inform performance context more than personal presidential causation.
Several retained items are still indirect because chapter 7B here is driven by corruption-adjacent conduct in the president's orbit rather than direct presidential self-dealing.
A few positive institutional actions are self-reported or appointment-based, so they support context more than proven outcomes.
The strongest adverse cluster is the 2022 adviser-corruption scandal plus repeated patronage/oversight concerns; broader governance evidence remains more mixed than any single incident suggests.
Much of the positive record is still self-reported or programmatic rather than independently audited execution.
Security and anti-corruption gains are partly offset by ongoing conflict, corruption allegations around the governing network, and incomplete transparency reforms.
Several useful items are official or advisory rather than outcome evidence, so confidence should stay moderated by corroboration gaps.
